title: A range of answers
objectives: Show an inequality on a number line with open and closed ends
Read an inequality back from a drawing
Read an inequality written with the number first

screens.prose: Here is a rule a number can pass or fail: $x > 3$, read “$x$ is bigger than 3”. Each dot is a whole number you can test.
screens.question: Tap every dot whose number makes $x > 3$ true.

hints.text: Test each dot in turn. Is its number bigger than 3?
Start with the dot at 3. Is 3 bigger than 3?
3 equals 3, so it fails. 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 are all bigger, so they pass.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each dot: a dot passes only if its number is bigger than 3.

byKey.took-three: You tapped 3 as well. But 3 is equal to 3, not bigger, so it fails.
byKey.below: You tapped the numbers below 3. The rule asks for numbers bigger than 3, to the right of it.
byKey.n3: You tapped 3. But 3 is equal to 3, not bigger, so it fails.
byKey.n2: 2 is smaller than 3, so it fails the rule.

explain.text: You kept 4 to 8 and dropped 3, because 3 is not bigger than itself. The dots that pass all lie to the right of 3. So far we have only tested whole numbers.

screens.prose: Whole numbers are not the only ones. Slide the test number $t$ along the line. Judge each spot against $x > 3$.
screens.question: How many numbers make $x > 3$ true?

options.why: You counted only the whole numbers. 3.5 and 3.1 are bigger than 3 too.

options.text: Every number above 3, too many to list

options.why: That takes in 3 itself. But 3 is not bigger than 3.
The line stops at 8 only because the drawing does. 20 and 1,000 pass too.

hints.text: Put $t$ at 3.5. Then at 3.1. Do they pass?

feedback.correct: Every number past 3 passes, however close to 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try decimals just past 3, and numbers far beyond 8.

explain.text: 3.1 passes, 3.01 passes, and so does 1,000. There are too many to list, so we draw them all at once: a bar from 3 to the right. The hollow dot at 3 shows that 3 itself is left out.

screens.prose: A rule like $x > 3$ is an **inequality**. The bar you just saw is its **solution set**: every number that passes. A hollow dot leaves its number out; a filled dot keeps it in.
screens.question: Which bar shows $x \ge 3$, read “$x$ is at least 3”?

options.why: B has a hollow dot, so it leaves 3 out. “At least 3” lets 3 in.
C runs left, to the numbers below 3. “At least 3” means 3 or more.

hints.text: Is 3 itself “at least 3”?
Two bars run to the right, A and B. Look at their dots.
3 is at least 3, so 3 is in: the dot is filled. Bigger numbers are in too, so the bar runs right.

feedback.correct: A filled dot at 3, and a bar running right.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide two things: is 3 in, and which way does the bar run?

explain.text: $x \ge 3$ lets 3 in, since 3 is at least 3. So the dot at 3 is filled. The bar still runs right, to every bigger number.

screens.prose: Now go the other way. Here is a drawing of a solution set.
screens.question: Which inequality does the drawing show?

options.why: That needs a filled dot. The hollow dot at −1 leaves −1 out.
The bar covers −2, −3 and so on. Those are smaller than −1, since they lie further left.
You read the boundary as 1. The dot sits at −1, left of 0.

hints.text: Is the dot hollow or filled?
Which way does the bar run from −1?
Hollow means −1 is out. Running left means smaller numbers. So $x$ is less than −1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the dot first, then the direction.

explain.text: The dot is hollow, so −1 is out. The bar runs left, where the numbers get smaller: −2 is less than −1. Together that reads $x < -1$.

screens.prose: The bar shows $x \ge -2.5$. Whole numbers here include 0 and negatives such as −2; exam papers call them **integers**. Some sit on the bar, and some do not.
screens.question: Drag the point to the smallest whole number in the solution set.

hints.text: Which whole numbers lie on the bar?
The bar starts at −2.5. Which whole number comes just after it?
−3 is left of −2.5, so it is off the bar. The next whole number to the right is −2.

feedback.correct: −2 is the first whole number on the bar.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the bar starts, then the first whole number to its right.

byKey.outside: −3 is left of −2.5, so it is off the bar. −3 is smaller than −2.5.
byKey.not-whole: −2.5 is in the set, but it is not a whole number.
byKey.too-big: That is on the bar, but there are smaller whole numbers on it. Move left.
byKey.p: Find where the bar starts, then the first whole number to its right.

explain.text: The bar starts at −2.5 with a filled dot. −3 lies to its left, so −3 fails. The first whole number on the bar is −2.

screens.prose: Inequalities can be written either way round. This one puts the number first: $-2 < x$.
screens.question: Which bar shows $-2 < x$?

options.why: You followed the symbol, which points left. But $-2 < x$ says $x$ is bigger than −2, so the bar runs right.
C has a filled dot, which lets −2 in. The symbol $<$ has no line under it, so −2 is out.

hints.text: Read it aloud: −2 is less than $x$. So is $x$ bigger or smaller than −2?
Test a number on bar A, such as −4. Is $-2 < -4$ true?
$-2 < x$ says the same as $x > -2$. Hollow dot at −2, bar running right.

feedback.correct: $-2 < x$ is $x > -2$: hollow at −2, running right.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn it round so $x$ comes first, then draw it.

byKey.A: You followed the way the symbol points. Test −4 from bar A: $-2 < -4$ is false.
byKey.C: You filled the dot at −2. The symbol $<$ has no line under it, so −2 is left out.

explain.text: The symbol is not an arrow. $-2 < x$ means −2 is smaller than $x$, so $x$ is bigger than −2. Swap the sides and the symbol together: $x > -2$.

screens.prose: There are four kinds in all. Each symbol tells you two things: the dot and the direction. $$x > a \qquad x \ge a \qquad x < a \qquad x \le a$$ A line under the symbol fills the dot. Bigger-than runs right; less-than runs left.
screens.question: Which drawing goes with $x \le 6$?

options.text: Filled dot at 6, bar running left
Hollow dot at 6, bar running left
options.why: The line under $\le$ lets 6 in, so the dot is filled.

options.text: Filled dot at 6, bar running right
options.why: Less than means smaller numbers, and those lie to the left.

feedback.correct: Filled, because 6 is in. Left, because the numbers are smaller.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the line under the symbol, then its direction.

explain.text: $x \le 6$ means 6 or anything smaller. The line under the symbol fills the dot at 6. Smaller numbers lie left, so the bar runs left.

screens.prose: You buy a share at £24.50. You set a stop-loss: the broker sells for you if the price $p$ falls to £22.00 or lower.
screens.question: Which inequality describes the prices that trigger the sale?

options.why: You left £22.00 out. The order fires at £22.00 too: “falls to £22.00 or lower”.
That covers every price at or above the stop, your £24.50 entry included. The sale is on the way down.
You used the entry price. Between £22.00 and £24.50 you still hold the share.

hints.text: Is £22.00 itself a trigger price?
The sale happens below the entry, on the way down.
“£22.00 or lower” includes £22.00 and every price under it: a filled dot at 22, running left.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide whether £22.00 is in, then which way the bar runs.

byKey.lt: You left out £22.00 itself. “Falls to £22.00 or lower” includes £22.00.

explain.text: “Or lower” includes £22.00, so the dot is filled. Lower prices lie to the left. The sale zone is everything from £22.00 down.

screens.prose: A second broker's stop fires only when $p < 22.00$. Prices move in steps of £0.01, called ticks.
screens.question: What is the highest price that fires this stop?

widget.label: Highest price that fires the stop

hints.text: Does £22.00 itself fire this stop?
The dot at 22 is hollow.
£22.00 is left out. The next price down is one tick lower.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. £22.00 is out; step down one tick of £0.01.

byKey.included: You used £22.00. The hollow end leaves £22.00 out, so the first price to fire is one tick lower.
byKey.tenth: You stepped down £0.10. A tick here is £0.01, so the price can stop at £21.99.

explain.text: With $p < 22.00$ the price must get below £22.00. Prices move in whole ticks of £0.01, so the highest such price is £21.99. A hollow end on a price line costs exactly one tick.

ideas: An inequality has a whole range of answers, too many to list. We draw them as a bar on the number line.
A filled dot keeps the boundary in ($\le$, $\ge$). A hollow dot leaves it out ($<$, $>$).
Read with $x$ first: $-2 < x$ is the same as $x > -2$, a bar running right.

formula.name: Reading an inequality
formula.note: Bigger-than runs right. A line under the symbol fills the dot.

summary.trap: The symbol is not an arrow. $-2 < x$ points left on the page, but its bar runs right.

quiz.question: Which of these numbers pass? Select all that apply.

options.why: −3.5 lies left of −3, so it is smaller than −3.
−4 lies left of −3. With negatives, the bigger digit is the smaller number.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Picture each number on the line, then compare it with −3.

explain.text: $x \ge -3$ lets −3 in and every number to its right. −2.5 and 0 are right of −3. −3.5 and −4 are to its left, so they fail.

quiz.prose: A solution set is drawn below.
quiz.question: Which inequality does it show?

options.why: The dot at 1.5 is filled, so 1.5 is in. That needs $\le$.
The bar runs left, towards smaller numbers. That is less than.
You rounded the boundary. The dot is at 1.5, halfway between 1 and 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the dot, then the direction.

explain.text: The filled dot puts 1.5 in the set. The bar runs left, to smaller numbers. So the drawing is $x \le 1.5$.

quiz.question: Which sentence says the same thing?

options.why: You read the symbol as pointing at $x$. But 7 is on the big side, so $x$ is the smaller one.
At most would let 7 in. The symbol $>$ has no line under it, so 7 is out.
This turns the meaning round and lets 7 in as well.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Swap the sides and turn the symbol with them.

explain.text: The open side of $>$ faces the bigger number, here 7. So $x$ is smaller than 7. Written with $x$ first, that is $x < 7$.

quiz.prose: Your desk lets you hold at most 400 shares of one stock. Let $n$ be the number you hold.
quiz.question: Which inequality is the limit?

options.why: That bans exactly 400 shares. “At most 400” allows 400 itself.
That says 400 or more. A limit caps the position from above.
That is the shares that would break the limit, not the ones allowed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide whether 400 itself is allowed.

explain.text: “At most 400” means 400 or fewer, so 400 is allowed. The symbol with a line under it is $\le$. The limit reads $n \le 400$.
